wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos
wine.classification: Grand Cru, one of the seven climats of the single Chablis Grand Cru appellation
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Parcels of Les Clos, the largest of the seven grand cru climats, on the hill that faces south west across the Serein from the town; stony limestone high on the slope, deeper clay lower down.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel tank, then moved to used oak casks, chiefly the traditional Chablis feuillette of 132 litres, with little or no new wood. The wine rests on its fine lees for a year to eighteen months before it is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Oyster shell, lemon pith and green apple over wet chalk, with a note of iodine; tight and dense, with high acidity and a long, saline finish that turns towards honey, hazelnut and dried mushroom with age.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first five to ten years, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass with a wide bowl.

label.means: The one appellation for the seven climats on the hill across the Serein from the town.
The climat, the largest of the seven, its name recalling the dry stone walls that once enclosed its vines.

records.table: From the largest of the seven Chablis grand cru climats, Raveneau's Les Clos is fermented in tank and raised in old casks with little or no new wood. Tight and saline when young, it needs years in bottle, so decant it and pour it cool rather than cold.
records.story: Chablis grew rich in the Middle Ages on wine shipped down the Yonne to Paris, and the Cistercian monks of Pontigny worked its slopes from the twelfth century; Les Clos may be the first kernel of their vineyard, and its name recalls the dry stone walls that once enclosed the vines. Phylloxera, war and frost shrank the district, and in 1938 the law gave the hill's seven climats a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. Ten years later the founder, whose name the domaine carries, married into the Dauvissat family, and the vines he had bought and the plots his wife's family held became one domaine. He was the first of his family to bottle his own wine, from the 1960s, and through the 1960s and 1970s, as grand cru land came up for sale, he bought parcels in Les Clos, Valmur and Blanchot. One son joined him in 1978 and a second followed, and they kept his method: fermentation in tank, then a year and more in old casks. In their cellar Les Clos shows that Chablis can be raised in wood and keep the taste of its limestone. On a list it belongs with the wines to cellar, not with the crisp aperitifs.

others.name: Chablis Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre
others.note: The premier cru that adjoins the grand cru hill, raised in old casks like the grands crus.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Valmur
others.note: The broadest of the domaine's grands crus, from the climat between Grenouilles and Les Clos.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Blanchot
others.note: From the climat at the south eastern end of the hill, beside Les Clos.

traps: Chablis Grand Cru is one appellation of seven climats on a single hill, not seven appellations or seven villages.
Raveneau is Chablis raised in old wood: call it neither steel fresh nor new oaked, since the old casks give texture rather than a taste of new oak.
Domaine Raveneau and Domaine Vincent Dauvissat are linked by marriage but are separate estates.

cards.front: Raveneau Les Clos: in what is it fermented, and in what is it then raised?
cards.back: Fermented in tank, then raised for a year and more in old oak casks, the Chablis feuillette among them.

cards.front: When was Domaine Raveneau founded, and how did its first vines come together?
cards.back: In 1948, when the founder married into the Dauvissat family and joined the vines he had bought to plots his wife's family held.

questions.q: A guest ordering Raveneau's Les Clos asks how it differs from the other Chablis grand cru climats. Which fact fits?
opts: It is the largest of the seven, facing south west
It is the smallest of the seven, between Vaudésir and Valmur
It is a premier cru that adjoins the grand cru hill
It is a walled monopole on the left bank of the Serein
questions.exp: Les Clos is the largest of the seven climats, on the south west facing hill above the Serein; Grenouilles is the smallest, and Montée de Tonnerre is the premier cru beside the hill.

The monks of Pontigny left them to the family

The appellation decree of 1938 granted them
questions.exp: The founder bought grand cru parcels in the 1960s and 1970s, as land came up for sale; 1923 is the cooperative's founding, and the decree of 1938 drew the appellation, not anyone's holdings.

wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Preuses
wine.classification: Grand Cru, one of the seven climats of the single Chablis Grand Cru appellation
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Les Preuses, between Bougros and Vaudésir towards the north western end of the grand cru hill on the right bank of the Serein, facing south and south west over the valley, on clay and limestone over Kimmeridgian marl; the vines are farmed organically.
wine.making: Raised in old oak, in barrels and the traditional Chablis feuillette of 132 litres, with little or no new wood, and left long on its lees, so the cask shapes the texture more than the flavour. It is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Lemon rind, crushed shell and white peach over chalk, rounder and more open than the house's Les Clos, with a quiet, creamy texture, bright acidity and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: More giving young than the house's Les Clos, it rewards ten years in bottle and keeps well beyond that in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly and an old one not at all; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: One appellation shared by the seven climats on the hill across the Serein from the town.
The climat, between Bougros and Vaudésir towards the north western end of the hill.
The name long printed on the domaine's labels, for the founder's son and grandson; the domaine is also known as Vincent Dauvissat.

records.table: Dauvissat's Les Preuses is a Chablis grand cru from the north western reach of the hill, raised in old casks and feuillettes with little or no new wood. It is rounder and more open than the house's Les Clos, yet stony and saline, and it rewards ten years in bottle.
records.story: Few Chablis growers bottled their own wine in 1931, when most sold it in cask to the merchants, but that year the founder of this domaine became one of the first to do so. In 1938 Chablis Grand Cru became an appellation, and the seven climats of the hill took one name on the label with their own beneath it. The founder's son was at work in the domaine from 1950, and his sister's marriage to the founder of Raveneau made the two families kin, so the domaines named together grew up side by side. The founder's grandson joined his father in 1976 and in time took charge. He kept the cellar as he found it: old barrels, the small Chablis feuillette, long lees ageing and little or no new oak, and in the early 2000s he turned the vineyards to organic farming. Les Preuses and Les Clos are the domaine's two grands crus, the first rounder and more open, the second firmer and slower. When a guest asks for Chablis raised in wood that keeps the taste of its limestone, Dauvissat is the other name beside Raveneau, and Les Preuses is the easier of its grands crus to open young.

others.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos
others.note: The domaine's other grand cru, firmer and slower to open than Les Preuses.

others.name: Chablis Premier Cru La Forest
others.note: The premier cru that is the house's calling card, spelled La Forest without an accent.

questions.q: Dauvissat and Raveneau are named together as the Chablis domaines that raise grand cru in wood. What links them?

A single owner who bought both in 1989

wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Bougros Côte Bouguerots
wine.classification: Grand Cru: a named parcel within Bougros, one of the seven climats of Chablis Grand Cru
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Côte Bouguerots, the steep, south facing lower slope of Bougros, the climat at the western end of the grand cru hill on the right bank of the Serein; poor soil over Kimmeridgian limestone and marl.
wine.making: Pressed gently and moved by gravity rather than pumped, it is fermented in stainless steel vats; a share of the wine that varies with the vintage then rests on its fine lees in French oak barrels several years old, never new, and the whole is brought together in steel before it is bottled at the domaine, well over a year after the harvest.
wine.glass: Lemon curd, ripe pear and sea spray over chalk, broad and ripe for a Chablis grand cru, with firm acidity, a supple middle and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Open within five years, it gains honey and hazelnut over the next ten and keeps longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with air in the glass; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The one appellation shared by the seven climats on the hill across the Serein.
The climat at the western end of the hill, one of the seven.
The steep lower slope within Bougros: a named part of the climat, not an eighth grand cru.

records.table: Steep even by the measure of the Chablis hill, Côte Bouguerots is the lower slope of Bougros that William Fèvre bottles under its own name. Fermented in steel and partly raised in old oak, never new, it is broad and ripe for Chablis, yet saline.
records.story: When the law drew the Chablis appellations in 1938, it gave the seven climats of the hill above the Serein one name, Chablis Grand Cru, but the district was in decline: phylloxera, war and frost had left only a fraction of its old vineyard planted, and the frost of 1957 took a whole crop. The domaine was founded in 1959 as the Domaine de la Maladière, by a grower whose family had long worked vines in Chablis, on the eve of the district's recovery, and over the decades that followed it came to hold one of the largest shares of grand cru in the district, in Les Clos, Bougros, Les Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir. Its founder favoured new oak, which divided opinion in a place that prizes the taste of its limestone. In 1998 the domaine passed to the Henriot family of Champagne, who had taken the helm of Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune in 1995. The new team set the new barrels aside and raised the grands crus in steel and older oak. Côte Bouguerots is the steep lower slope of Bougros, and the house bottles it under its own name, so that a guest can taste one slope within a climat. Here a large domaine's grand cru tastes of the hill, not of the cellar.

wine.name: Chablis Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Montée de Tonnerre, the premier cru on the right bank of the Serein just set back from the grand cru hill, across from Blanchot; west facing slopes of shallow soil over Kimmeridgian marly limestone.
wine.making: Fermented with its own yeasts in stainless steel tanks and aged in steel on its fine lees for a year or more, with no oak at any stage, as every wine of the domaine is, then bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon zest and wet chalk with a note of crushed shell, taut and pure with no trace of wood, high acidity and a long, saline finish; age brings honey and toasted hazelnut.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready after three or four years, it gains depth over ten years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of moderate size.

label.means: The tier between Chablis and Chablis Grand Cru, with the climat named after it.
The climat, across from the grand cru Blanchot on the right bank of the Serein.
The name on the labels: Louis Michel and sons, the family domaine.

records.table: Not a stave of oak touches Louis Michel's Montée de Tonnerre: this Chablis premier cru from beside the grand cru hill is fermented and aged in steel alone. It is pure, taut and saline, with nothing between the fruit and the limestone, so pour it with oysters or white fish.
records.story: The family counts its beginnings from 1850, when it planted its first vines in Chablis, then a busy vineyard sending its wine to Paris by river. The decades that followed were hard: phylloxera, wars and spring frosts left only a fraction of the old vineyard standing, and when the law drew its appellations in 1938 the district was at a low ebb. Recovery came after the frost of 1957, when heaters and sprinklers let growers plant again, and through it the Michel family took the opposite road from the old barrel domaines. Until then their wines had been made in old oak; from the end of the 1960s they turned to steel, and by about 1980 the last barrels were gone, so that every wine of the house, grand cru included, is fermented and aged in stainless steel. Their argument is that Chablis needs nothing from wood: the cold climate and the Kimmeridgian marl give the acidity, the salt and the shell, and steel keeps them clear. Montée de Tonnerre, the premier cru across from the grand cru hill, is where that argument is heard at its fullest. Poured beside a Raveneau or a Dauvissat from the same ground, it shows a guest what the cellar changes and what the vineyard does not.

wine.name: Chablis Grand Cru Château Grenouilles
wine.classification: Grand Cru, from Grenouilles, one of the seven climats of Chablis Grand Cru
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, as every Chablis must be.
wine.sites: Château Grenouilles, a single block of vines covering most of Grenouilles, the smallest of the seven climats, between Vaudésir and Valmur on the right bank of the Serein, on clay and limestone over Kimmeridgian marl.
wine.making: The must is settled cold, then fermented and taken through its malolactic partly in oak barrels and partly in tank; the wine rests on its fine lees, in barrel and tank, for well over a year before the cooperative bottles it under the château's name.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon peel and white blossom over chalk dust, with a cool sea breeze note, a supple, rounded middle and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Open after four or five years, it gains honey and hazelnut over ten and keeps longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate in Grenouilles whose wine the cooperative bottles apart; a cooperative's wine, not a private grower's.
The one appellation shared by the seven climats on the hill.
The Chablis growers' cooperative, founded in 1923, which makes and bottles the wine.

records.table: Château Grenouilles is La Chablisienne's grand cru, from most of Grenouilles, the smallest of the seven Chablis climats. Fermented in barrel and tank and long on its lees, it is supple and saline, and it shows what a cooperative of growers can bottle at grand cru level.
records.story: In the hard years after the First World War, when Chablis wine was difficult to sell, a group of growers led by a priest joined together in 1923 to make and sell their wine as one, and La Chablisienne was born. Fifteen years later, in 1938, the law gave the seven climats of the grand cru hill a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. The cooperative grew with the district's recovery after the frosts of the 1950s, until its members farmed a large share of the appellation. Grenouilles is the smallest of the seven climats, set between Vaudésir and Valmur beside the Serein; its name, written as early as 1321, means frogs. Most of it lies in one block, Château Grenouilles, an estate the cooperative took on in 2003, by its own account, and whose wine it bottles apart under the château's name. That a grand cru should come from a cooperative surprises many guests, and it is a question a candidate meets. Château Grenouilles is the proof that Chablis Grand Cru is not the wine of small domaines alone.

report: Rechecked with search on 12 November 2026: the founding of 1923 by growers led by a priest, in the hard inter-war years, and Château Grenouilles as a single block of most of the climat between Vaudésir and Valmur, which the cooperative has held since 2003, are the cooperative's own pages, with Wikipedia for the founding.

Wikipedia says the cooperative bought Château Grenouilles in 1999; the cooperative's own page and a merchant say 2003, so the story says 2003 as the cooperative tells it, and the integrator may prefer to leave the year out.

The making is the cooperative's own sheets for 2021 and 2022: cold settling, both fermentations in barrel and tank, about fourteen months on fine lees in barrel and tank; sheets for 2007 and 2015 give twenty months, so the record says well over a year.
The priest, the abbé Balitrand in the cooperative's account, is described, not named: his dates were not found. The day of the founding, 1 May, is in Wikipedia alone and is out.
Grenouilles as the smallest climat, its place on the hill, its name for the frogs and the year 1321 are the Chablis wine body's own page.

The library's Les Vénérables Vieilles Vignes is shown on the cooperative's shop as Les Vénérables, with no Vieilles Vignes found, so the others line says Chablis Les Vénérables; Les Preuses is replaced by Pas si Petit, which the cooperative's own sheet confirms.

changed: story: the growers joined in 1923 in the hard inter-war years, led by a priest, as the cooperative's own page tells it, where the record said phylloxera had taken most of the vines and the growers sold to merchants; the cooperative took on Château Grenouilles in 2003 by its own account, a single block of most of the climat, where the record said only that its vines were worked by the cooperative; the name Grenouilles is written as early as 1321, by the Chablis wine body.

making: cold settling, both fermentations partly in oak barrels and partly in tank, then well over a year on fine lees in barrel and tank, by the cooperative's sheets, where the record said only vinified apart and many months on the lees.
sites: a single block between Vaudésir and Valmur on the right bank, on clay and limestone over Kimmeridgian marl, by the cooperative's page and sheet.
table: the claim that it is ready sooner than the barrel domaines is taken out, unsourced; the wine is fermented in barrel and tank and long on its lees.
